description: Using engineering, coding, and our understanding of space to make the change we want to see!
summary:
You were built for ninety sols. You stayed for fourteen years.

Last Light is an emotional 3D browser game about NASA’s Opportunity rover and the discoveries worth sending home. Players become Oppy, driving across Mars, investigating rocks, and photographing a world no human has visited. Each discovery connects to real NASA imagery and the science that helped reveal Mars’s watery past.

Over time, the familiar rhythm of exploring and sending messages home becomes something to care about. Then a dust storm begins to take away the sunlight. The music fades beneath the wind. Eventually, the player finds themselves on Earth, sending a call and waiting for an answer.

Created for “Abandoned but not Forgotten,” Last Light introduces school-age and casual space enthusiasts to Opportunity’s hardware, discoveries, and legacy. We want players to understand what this small rover accomplished, feel the distance it crossed to share those discoveries, and remember it after the screen goes dark.
details:
We built Last Light around a feeling: getting used to hearing from someone, then realizing they might never answer again.

Opportunity spent fourteen years exploring Mars and sending discoveries back to Earth. That history gave us the foundation for an emotional, interactive story about curiosity, routine, and connection. We wanted players to spend time doing Oppy’s work, finding something interesting in the rocks, looking a little closer, and deciding it was worth sending home.

Last Light is a playable 3D browser game designed for a roughly 10 to 15 minute experience. Players drive through a reconstructed Martian landscape, investigate evidence of ancient water, photograph discoveries, and transmit their findings to Earth. It is available at https://orion-north.github.io/last-light/.

The science is part of what the player does. At Last Chance, players trace crossing rock layers and examine patterns associated with ancient flowing water. At Berry Bowl, they brush dust from a surface and compare qualitative readings from exposed rock and grain-rich material. These interactions introduce the relationship between an instrument, an observation, and the conclusions scientists can draw from it. They are based on NASA’s accounts of the discoveries, with the procedures simplified for an approachable game.

Photography brings the player’s experience into contact with the real mission. Looking through Oppy’s camera, the player frames a discovery in the world they have been exploring. The captured view then gives way to an authentic NASA image before the finding is sent home. There is something moving about that transition. The player has just found something in a game, and suddenly they are looking at what Opportunity actually saw.

Our research began with the Spirit and Opportunity mission resource listed in the challenge. NASA and JPL mission histories, instrument descriptions, and discovery images informed the investigations and historical events. The rover itself uses NASA’s textured 3D model. Credits and source references are available in the game and repository, and the photographic reveals distinguish our reconstructed environment from the original observations.

The emotional story grows through repetition. Early in the journey, sending a discovery brings a reassuring response. The player learns that someone is listening. As the storm develops, dust blocks the sunlight, the world darkens, and the wind gradually overwhelms the music. Oppy’s imagined thoughts appear as terminal-style text, accompanied by small electronic tones that change with the emotion of each line. The dialogue moves from curiosity to reassurance and, finally, exhaustion.

Eventually, the perspective shifts to Earth. The player sits at a recovery workstation and sends a call toward the rover they have come to know. The communication animation is familiar by this point. They know where the reply should appear.

This time, it does not.

The ending gives space to remember what Opportunity accomplished. A personal archive carries forward the discoveries and memories selected during the journey. We wanted the last feeling to include gratitude for the work, the knowledge, and the years that nobody originally expected.

This directly addresses the challenge’s invitation to help younger and casual audiences connect with the hardware left beyond Earth. We chose to focus closely on one rover, giving players time to understand its purpose and care about its contribution. Cameras, scientific tools, communications, and solar power all have a role in the experience. The intended educational impact is to help players understand how a machine on another planet could gather evidence about its past, and encourage them to explore the real mission afterward.

We developed Last Light using JavaScript, HTML, CSS, Three.js, and WebGL 2. The Web Audio API produces the original adaptive score, wind, communication sounds, and dialogue tones. Development and verification used Node.js, Git, GitHub, automated tests, and browser-based checks. The game supports keyboard and mouse input and compatible controllers, with no installation or account required.

We considered scientific accuracy, accessibility, and emotional pacing throughout development. The primary audience is school-age learners around twelve and older, alongside casual space enthusiasts. Local progress saving, changing input prompts, reduced-motion settings, and sound-off support help accommodate different ways of playing. Optional memories and sources let interested players explore the science without interrupting every moment of the story.

Opportunity’s thoughts are fictional, and the terrain and instrument interactions are artistic reconstructions. The discoveries and historical events are grounded in NASA sources. Player choices shape what they remember, while the mission’s historical outcome remains intact.

We hope players leave remembering a rock they examined, a picture they sent, or the moment they waited for a reply. Those small experiences are our way of helping Opportunity’s story stay with them.
